title: The 9 Biggest Classroom Management Mistakes Teachers Make
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin presents a self-assessment list of nine common classroom management mistakes, framed as a diagnostic tool teachers can use to evaluate their own practice on a five-point scale. The mistakes include inconsistently enforcing rules, relying on lecturing and pleading instead of consequences, taking misbehavior personally, yelling, teaching the classroom management plan through preaching rather than modeling and practice, withholding warmth and personality for fear of losing control, using false or manipulative praise, maintaining consequences too weak to matter, and talking so much that routines never become automatic. He argues that inconsistent rule enforcement is by far the most damaging and common mistake, since every unenforced violation seeds future misbehavior. The piece closes by encouraging teachers to score themselves honestly on each item and work toward eliminating the mistakes entirely.
points: Inconsistent enforcement of classroom rules is identified as the single most common and damaging classroom management mistake.
Relying on lecturing, pleading, and reminders instead of enforced consequences undermines a classroom management plan's effectiveness.
Withholding warmth and personality out of fear of losing authority actually weakens the rapport that authority depends on.
False or strategically deployed praise is dishonest and ultimately ineffective because students recognize insincerity.
A self-scoring exercise (rating each mistake 1 to 5) is offered as a practical tool for ongoing self-improvement.
quotes: Not enforcing classroom rules 100% of the time. This is by far the biggest mistake, and it's a common problem for a majority of teachers. For every time you let something go, you create more misbehavior in the future.

Taking poor student behavior personally. Revenge isn't sweet, it's self-sabotage. Letting your emotions get involved in classroom management will cloud your judgment, make you do things you will regret, and alienate your students.

Not smiling or showing your personality the first month, semester, or, for some, the entire school year. Likability is the key to building rapport. And rapport makes everything easier, especially classroom management.
But false praise doesn’t change behavior; it’s a momentary fix devoid of meaning. Students are perceptive and see right through inauthenticity.
Your students should know exactly what to do, and be busy doing it, every minute of the school day. Otherwise, their eyes will glaze over, and they’ll grow tired of you and your shtick.
Work on raising each score to a 5, and I think you’ll be a happier and more successful teacher.
